text: Welcome to your bistro! Pick any recipe on today's menu and buy what it needs: {examples}. Each food's category must match the slot exactly; flip a card to see its category. Explore the stores and shelves, then drag packages into your cart. You may buy extras, but checkout must be affordable and leave you enough ingredients for at least one recipe. Open the cart to remove packages. Pantry and Recipes remain available at any time.

Before cooking, sort the new foods into Green, Yellow or Red. These are the game's Traffic Light groups: Green foods are the everyday foundation and the only foods that build health. Yellow foods are ones customers are moving away from. Red foods are the ones to avoid. Flip cards to inspect ingredients. Each new food you sort correctly gives back {maxDiscount} of what you paid for it today. Foods you already know and wrong answers give nothing back. You can rearrange cards before submitting. There is no retry after submission; a wrong food can return on a later purchase.
Let's cook the ingredients you prepared. Choose any recipe you have ingredients for. You can still inspect your pantry or return to the main menu.

Drag one serving at a time into the recipe slots. Required slots need the exact category and count. Optional slots may stay empty, or be filled exactly. A red rim means something needs attention. Open a slot to drag a serving back out. Review the dish whenever you like; this first lesson requires a successful recipe before you can confirm serving.

Your first recipe is built! You used {ingredients}. This dish changed health by {healthDelta} and covered these Daily Dozen groups: {dailyDozen}. In this game, Green servings and the Daily Dozen groups they cover contribute to health. Each Daily Dozen group a guest has not eaten before adds extra health for them; groups they have already had add nothing extra, so vary the plants you serve each guest. Positive health gains per dish are capped. Aim for variety within the recipe's slots, rather than piling on extra servings. From now on, you may also serve imperfect recipes and face their consequences.

You have now heard both sides of a rush and crash. A brief lift can feel encouraging, yet it may not last. Watch the customer's experience over time. Here, rush/crash is visual and dialogue feedback: it adds no extra health penalty beyond the dish's normal calculation. Think about the ingredients and the overall meal, rather than treating a burst of energy as proof of a good result.

A letter from the landlord: the opening grace period ends tomorrow. From tomorrow morning, rent of ${rent} is charged every day before the market opens, even on a quiet day. Your money can dip below zero, but you can only shop while your balance is positive, so keep a cushion. A popular bistro also earns walk-in takeaway each evening, so delighting guests is what keeps the lights on. Guests will soon bring requests too: answering them builds popularity, and ignoring them costs some.

Money is running low: tomorrow's rent of ${rent} could push you below zero, and below zero the shops won't take your order. You can raise cash by selling food you won't use: open Pantry and drag servings onto SELL, then press Sell. Each serving sells for {sellRate} of its lowest shelf price (or of what you paid, if that was less). Food that would spoil before you can cook it is the best thing to sell.

From today, guests may arrive with a request such as Savory, Creamy or Crunchy. Each recipe on the menu lists what it is good for. Serving a recipe that answers a guest's request delights them and grows your popularity much faster; leaving a request unanswered costs some popularity. Health still comes only from the foods you choose. Comfort is answered by any complete recipe with an average ingredient appeal of at least {comfort}.

Your pantry can't complete any recipe on the menu, so a local farmer has stepped in with a small crate of plain staples: enough for one simple dish. The farmer helps at most once a day, and only when nothing on the menu can be made. Gifted food spoils after a day and has low appeal, so guests won't be thrilled. Shop, or sell food you won't use, to get back on your feet.

Your bistro has {totalDays} days to make its name. Each day you shop at the market, sort what you bought, then cook for your guests. Rent of ${rent} is charged every morning from day {rentStart}, and guests start bringing requests on day {cravingsStart}. After day {totalDays}, your popularity and the community's wellbeing decide how the story ends.

Popularity is how well known your bistro is. It decides how many guests come each day: more seats open at {guestThresholds} popularity, up to {maxGuests} guests. Above {walkInThreshold}, walk-in customers also buy takeaway every evening, about ${walkInPer100} for each 100 points above it. Delighted guests, answered requests and tasty plates raise it; mismatched dishes and ignored requests lower it.

Your wallet pays for food at the market, and guests pay you, plus tips, for every dish you serve. From day {rentStart}, rent of ${rent} is charged every morning. Your money can dip below zero, but stores only take orders while you have money, and ending the run deep in debt closes the bistro. Short on cash? Sell food you won't use from the Pantry for {sellRate} of its price.
